title: 1997 AHSME Problem 8
statement: Mientka Publishing Company prices its best seller Where’s Walter? as follows: \[ C(n)= \begin{cases} 12n, & 1\le n\le24,\\ 11n, & 25\le n\le48,\\ 10n, & 49\le n, \end{cases} \] where \(n\) is the number of books ordered, and \(C(n)\) is the cost in dollars of \(n\) books. Notice that \(25\) books cost less than \(24\) books. For how many values of \(n\) is it cheaper to buy more than \(n\) books than to buy exactly \(n\) books?

solutions.text: At the first break, \(C(25)=275\) is below \(C(23)=276\) and \(C(24)=288,\) giving \(n=23\) and \(n=24.\) At the second, \(C(49)=490\) is below \(C(n)=11n\) for \(n=45,\) \(n=46,\) \(n=47,\) \(n=48.\) No other \(n\) works because each piece increases. There are \(2+4=6,\) so D is correct.
hints: Only the two price-break points can make a larger order cheaper
Compare \(C(n)\) with \(C(25)\) near the first break and with \(C(49)\) near the second
